sourceNote: Selective DGT editorial notes for Romans 1–8.

1:4: ὁρισθέντος can mean appointed, designated, or marked out. DGT uses “appointed Son of God in power” without implying that Jesus first became God’s Son only at the resurrection.
1:17: ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν is literally “from faith into faith.” DGT keeps the compact wording because interpretations such as “from first to last by faith” go beyond the Greek phrase itself.
1:26: Paul contrasts φυσικὴ χρῆσις, “natural relations/use,” with what is παρὰ φύσιν, “contrary to nature.” DGT retains that contrast without expanding Paul’s argument beyond the wording here.
2:6: Paul states that God “will repay each person according to their works.” DGT leaves the statement in its full force and does not harmonize it in the translation with later statements about justification by faith.
2:13: δικαιωθήσονται is future passive: “will be justified.” DGT preserves the forensic verb rather than weakening it to “will be considered good.”
3:22: πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ can grammatically be read as “faith in Jesus Christ” or “faithfulness of Jesus Christ.” DGT uses the traditional objective reading in the main text while noting the genitive ambiguity.
3:25: ἱλαστήριον can refer to an atoning means or the “mercy seat”/atonement cover. DGT uses “atoning place” to keep both the sacrificial and sanctuary resonance visible.
3:28: “Works of law” translates ἔργων νόμου without adding the article “the” before law. DGT keeps Paul’s compact formulation rather than defining in the translation exactly which works are in view.
4:3: ἐλογίσθη, “was counted/reckoned,” is a key verb throughout the chapter. DGT consistently uses “counted” to keep Paul’s repeated accounting metaphor visible.
4:25: The two διά clauses are parallel: Jesus was handed over “because of” our trespasses and raised “because of” our justification. The exact causal nuance of the second clause is debated; DGT keeps the same preposition in both.
5:1: SBLGNT reads ἔχομεν, “we have peace.” A well-known variant reads ἔχωμεν, “let us have peace.” DGT follows the displayed SBLGNT indicative.
5:12: ἐφ’ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον can mean “because all sinned” and has also received other interpretations. DGT uses the causal reading while keeping the Adam-to-all structure of Paul’s sentence.
5:18: Paul’s parallel extends “to all people” on both sides of the comparison. DGT translates the scope directly without importing a theological qualification into the wording itself.
6:7: δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας literally uses the verb “has been justified” from sin. Many translations render the sense “freed from sin”; DGT keeps “justified” so Paul’s wording remains visible.
6:19: ἁγιασμόν can mean sanctification or holiness. DGT uses “sanctification” here to preserve the process/result noun used again in verse 22.
7:6: πνεύματος can be translated “spirit” or “Spirit.” DGT capitalizes it here because of the contrast with “letter” and the broader Pauline context, though Greek manuscripts do not mark capitalization in this way.
7:14: The textual tradition includes σάρκινος/σάρκινος-type variation in spelling and nuance. DGT follows the displayed SBLGNT sense “fleshly,” not “spiritual.”
7:15: γινώσκω here can mean “understand/recognize,” not merely “know.” DGT uses “understand” because Paul is describing his inability to make sense of what he produces.
8:1: SBLGNT ends the verse after “Christ Jesus.” The familiar longer wording about walking “not according to flesh but according to Spirit” belongs to verse 4 in the earliest form and is absent from the SBLGNT text of verse 1.
8:2: SBLGNT reads the singular pronoun σε, “you,” rather than με, “me,” in “set you free.” DGT follows the displayed Greek text.
8:15: υἱοθεσία literally refers to placement as sons/adoption. DGT uses “adoption,” while verse 16 immediately uses the broader term τέκνα, “children.”
8:28: SBLGNT reads πάντα συνεργεῖ, “all things work together,” with God not explicitly stated as the grammatical subject. DGT keeps that wording rather than supplying “God causes all things.”
8:29: προέγνω and προώρισεν are translated “foreknew” and “predestined.” DGT preserves the verbs without defining the theological relationship between foreknowledge, predestination, and human response.
8:34: The verse is a sequence of rhetorical clauses: Christ died, was raised, is at God’s right hand, and intercedes. DGT keeps the structure rather than turning it into a doctrinal summary.
9:5: The final clause can be punctuated in more than one way. DGT takes ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων, θεὸς εὐλογητός as referring to Christ: “the one who is over all, God blessed forever.”
9:13: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” quotes Malachi 1 in a corporate/covenantal context. DGT translates the verbs directly and leaves the scope of Paul’s application to the argument.
9:16: The sentence is literally “not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of God showing mercy.” DGT preserves the contrast without adding a theory of how divine mercy relates to human willing elsewhere in Romans.
9:22: κατηρτισμένα, “prepared/fitted,” is a perfect passive participle without an explicit agent. DGT does not insert “God prepared” into the clause.
10:4: τέλος can mean end, goal, culmination, or completion. DGT uses “end of the law,” while Paul’s intended nuance remains debated.
10:9: The Greek is compact: “confess with your mouth Lord Jesus.” DGT makes the predication explicit as “Jesus is Lord” without changing the confession’s content.
10:17: SBLGNT reads ῥήματος Χριστοῦ, “word of Christ.” A familiar variant reads θεοῦ, “of God.” DGT follows the displayed SBLGNT text.
11:5: “A remnant according to election of grace” is Paul’s wording. DGT keeps both election and grace explicit without explaining their theological relationship in the translation.
11:20: Paul tells Gentile believers, “you stand by faith… do not think high things, but fear.” DGT preserves the warning directly.
11:22: The condition ἐὰν ἐπιμένῃς, “if you remain/continue,” is explicit. DGT retains the conditional force rather than smoothing it away.
11:25: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in” marks a temporal limit to Israel’s partial hardening. DGT leaves “fullness” untranslated into a numerical or qualitative theory.
11:26: καὶ οὕτως means “and in this way/so.” DGT uses “in this way all Israel will be saved,” avoiding the stronger temporal paraphrase “and then.”
11:32: Paul says God “shut up all in disobedience so that he might show mercy to all.” DGT keeps both occurrences of “all” without adding a restriction into the verse itself.
12:1: λογικὴ λατρεία can mean reasonable, rational, or spiritual service/worship. DGT uses “reasonable service,” preserving the adjective’s connection to reason.
12:2: αἰών means age rather than necessarily “world.” DGT therefore uses “this age” in “do not be conformed to this age.”
13:1: The passage says governing authorities are ordered/appointed by God. DGT translates the claim directly without turning it into an assertion that every act of every ruler is divinely approved.
13:4: μάχαιρα is literally “sword.” DGT retains the concrete image rather than paraphrasing it as a generic “power to punish.”
14:10: SBLGNT reads “the judgment seat of God.” A well-known variant reads “of Christ.” DGT follows the displayed SBLGNT text.
14:14: κοινός here means common/unclean in the ritual or conscience sense. DGT uses “unclean” for readability while the underlying word is literally “common.”
14:23: The chapter closes with the broad maxim “everything not from faith is sin.” DGT keeps its scope as written rather than narrowing it only to food disputes.
15:16: Paul describes his ministry with priestly language: λειτουργός and ἱερουργοῦντα. DGT renders this “minister… serving as a priest of the good news” so the metaphor is visible.
16:1: διάκονον can mean servant, minister, or deacon. DGT uses “servant” in the main text while leaving the question of formal office open.
16:2: προστάτις can mean patron, benefactor, or protector. DGT uses “patron,” reflecting Phoebe’s recognized support of many, including Paul.
16:7: Ἰουνίαν is naturally the female name Junia. ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις can mean “notable among the apostles” or “well known to the apostles.” DGT uses the former while noting the construction is discussed.
16:22: Tertius explicitly identifies himself as the one who wrote the letter, indicating his role as Paul’s amanuensis/scribe.
16:24: Romans 16:24 is absent from important early witnesses and is bracketed in the SBLGNT tradition. DGT includes it because it appears in the displayed base text, while flagging the textual uncertainty.
